entries.title: “Iscariot”: of Kerioth?
entries.text: “Iscariot” is most often explained as “man of Kerioth”, a town of Judah (Joshua 15:25), though Smith (1884) notes that the name has received many interpretations. Scripture does not say where he came from.

entries.title: He had the bag

entries.title: Son of Simon

entries.title: Whose name is Iscariot?
entries.text: The Greek texts differ at John 6:71. In the Textus Receptus behind the KJV, Iscariot belongs to Judas; in Tischendorf's text it belongs to Simon, and the Revised Version (1881) follows that reading: Judas the son of Simon Iscariot. On that reading the father too was called Iscariot.

accounts.title: Named as the betrayer at the supper

verses.text: Now when the even was come, he sat down with the twelve.
And as they did eat, he said, Verily I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me.
And they were exceeding sorrowful, and began every one of them to say unto him, Lord, is it I?
And he answered and said, He that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me.
The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born.
Then Judas, which betrayed him, answered and said, Master, is it I? He said unto him, Thou hast said.
And as they sat and did eat, Jesus said, Verily I say unto you, One of you which eateth with me shall betray me.
And they began to be sorrowful, and to say unto him one by one, Is it I? and another said, Is it I?
And he answered and said unto them, It is one of the twelve, that dippeth with me in the dish.
The Son of man indeed goeth, as it is written of him: but woe to that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! good were it for that man if he had never been born.
¶ But, behold, the hand of him that betrayeth me is with me on the table.
And truly the Son of man goeth, as it was determined: but woe unto that man by whom he is betrayed!
And they began to enquire among themselves, which of them it was that should do this thing.
When Jesus had thus said, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me.
Then the disciples looked one on another, doubting of whom he spake.
Now there was leaning on Jesus’ bosom one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved.
Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, that he should ask who it should be of whom he spake.
He then lying on Jesus’ breast saith unto him, Lord, who is it?
Jesus answered, He it is, to whom I shall give a sop, when I have dipped it. And when he had dipped the sop, he gave it to Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon.
And after the sop Satan entered into him. Then said Jesus unto him, That thou doest, do quickly.
Now no man at the table knew for what intent he spake this unto him.
For some of them thought, because Judas had the bag, that Jesus had said unto him, Buy those things that we have need of against the feast; or, that he should give something to the poor.
He then having received the sop went immediately out: and it was night.
¶ And while he yet spake, lo, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and elders of the people.
Now he that betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast.
And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him.
And Jesus said unto him, Friend, wherefore art thou come? Then came they, and laid hands on Jesus, and took him.
¶ And immediately, while he yet spake, cometh Judas, one of the twelve, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders.
And he that betrayed him had given them a token, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he; take him, and lead him away safely.
And as soon as he was come, he goeth straightway to him, and saith, Master, master; and kissed him.
¶ And they laid their hands on him, and took him.
¶ And while he yet spake, behold a multitude, and he that was called Judas, one of the twelve, went before them, and drew near unto Jesus to kiss him.
But Jesus said unto him, Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?
And Judas also, which betrayed him, knew the place: for Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples.
Judas then, having received a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons.
Jesus therefore, knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye?
They answered him, Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus saith unto them, I am he. And Judas also, which betrayed him, stood with them.
Now the names of the twelve apostles are these; The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;
Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.
And Simon he surnamed Peter;
And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder:
And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Canaanite,
And Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him: and they went into an house.
Simon, (whom he also named Peter,) and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew,
Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphæus, and Simon called Zelotes,
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.

John three times calls him “the son of Simon” or “Simon's son”.
At the supper Peter asked the disciple whom Jesus loved to find out who the betrayer was; after Judas's death Peter proposed that another take his place.

family.text: His father was Simon: “Judas Iscariot the son of Simon”.

The Greek texts differ at John 6:71. In the Textus Receptus behind the KJV, Iscariot belongs to Judas; in Tischendorf's text it belongs to Simon, and the Revised Version (1881) follows that reading: Judas the son of Simon Iscariot. On that reading the father too was called Iscariot.

identifications.text: Every list of the Twelve names him “Judas Iscariot” and adds that he betrayed Jesus, which sets him apart from the other Judas among the Twelve.

scripture.text: Matthew: when Judas saw that Jesus “was condemned”, he “repented himself”, brought back the thirty pieces of silver and said, “I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood”. He “cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.”
Matthew: the chief priests would not put “the price of blood” into the treasury. They “bought with them the potter's field, to bury strangers in”, and so it was called “The field of blood”.

Acts, in Peter's words: “this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.” The field was called “Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood.”

Each account quotes Scripture: Matthew the words “spoken by Jeremy the prophet” about the thirty pieces of silver and the potter's field; Acts two Psalms, “Let his habitation be desolate” and “his bishoprick let another take”.

The two accounts stand side by side here and are not merged. They differ on who bought the field (the chief priests in Matthew, Judas himself in Acts) and on how he died (he “hanged himself” in Matthew; “falling headlong, he burst asunder” in Acts). Mark, Luke and John say nothing of his death.

tradition.text: Papias tells a third story, which Kerr (ISBE, 1915) calls “a legendary account”: Judas's body swelled until he could not pass where a chariot could pass easily, and he was crushed by the chariot, “so that his bowels gushed out”.

items.q: How did Judas die? Matthew and Acts tell it differently.
items.full: How did Judas die? Matthew and Acts tell it differently. (Harmonising views first, as Strauss lists them, then the view that they differ.)

views.label: He hanged himself, then the body fell and burst
views.holders: Easton (1897), quoting an earlier writer; Casaubon, Kuinoel, Winer and others, as listed by Strauss (1846); the Latin Vulgate's wording of Acts 1:18, “when he had hanged himself”, as reported by Kerr (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: Easton: the rope gave way or the branch broke, and he fell headlong and was crushed. Acts tells the end of what Matthew begins.

views.label: “Hanged himself” means he was choked, and then fell
views.holders: Matthew Henry (early 18th century), following Henry Hammond

argument.text: Henry takes Matthew's word to mean that Judas was “strangled, or choked with grief and horror”, after which he fell headlong and burst.

views.label: He survived the hanging and died later
views.holders: Oecumenius and other ancient commentators, as reported by Strauss (1846)

argument.text: On this view Matthew tells of a failed attempt, and Acts of the death that came afterwards.

views.label: Two different accounts
views.holders: D. F. Strauss (1846), with K. Hase

argument.text: Strauss argues that each writer knew only the story he tells, since otherwise he could not have left out the other half, and judges the attempts to reconcile them a failure.

items.full: Who bought the field? (In the order Strauss discusses them.)

views.label: The priests bought it with his money, so Acts can say he acquired it
views.holders: Matthew Henry (early 18th century); harmonists reported by Strauss (1846)

argument.text: Henry: “He did not purchase the field, but the wages of his unrighteousness did”.
In Matthew the chief priests buy the field after his death, and it is named for the blood of Jesus on the money; in Acts Judas buys it and it is named for his own blood.

argument.text: Matthew: when Judas saw that Jesus “was condemned”, he “repented himself”, brought back the thirty pieces of silver and said, “I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood”. He “cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.”

The two accounts stand side by side here and are not merged. They differ on who bought the field (the chief priests in Matthew, Judas himself in Acts) and on how he died (he “hanged himself” in Matthew; “falling headlong, he burst asunder” in Acts). Mark, Luke and John say nothing of his death.

argument.text: Papias tells a third story, which Kerr (ISBE, 1915) calls “a legendary account”: Judas's body swelled until he could not pass where a chariot could pass easily, and he was crushed by the chariot, “so that his bowels gushed out”.

items.q: Beyond these verses Scripture gives no reason for the betrayal: John says he “was a thief, and had the bag” (John 12:6); Luke says “Then entered Satan into Judas” (Luke 22:3), and John that the devil put it into his heart and Satan entered into him (John 13:2, 27); Matthew records his question “What will ye give me?” (Matthew 26:15). This page adds no motive of its own.
Scripture does not say where he came from, or what “Iscariot” means.
Mark, Luke and John do not tell how Judas died.

verses.43018001: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples.
verses.43018002: And Judas also, which betrayed him, knew the place: for Jesus ofttimes resorted thither with his disciples.
verses.43018003: Judas then, having received a band of men and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, cometh thither with lanterns and torches and weapons.
verses.43018004: Jesus therefore, knowing all things that should come upon him, went forth, and said unto them, Whom seek ye?
verses.43018005: They answered him, Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus saith unto them, I am he. And Judas also, which betrayed him, stood with them.
verses.44001016: Men and brethren, this scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Holy Ghost by the mouth of David spake before concerning Judas, which was guide to them that took Jesus.
verses.44001017: For he was numbered with us, and had obtained part of this ministry.
verses.44001018: Now this man purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out.
verses.44001019: And it was known unto all the dwellers at Jerusalem; insomuch as that field is called in their proper tongue, Aceldama, that is to say, The field of blood.
verses.44001020: For it is written in the book of Psalms, Let his habitation be desolate, and let no man dwell therein: and his bishoprick let another take.
verses.44001025: That he may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place.
